titre: Counting to Ten, Without Getting There
accroche: For months, Daniel Everett tries to teach Pirahã people in the Amazon to count. None of his students reaches ten.
contenu_vulgarise:
Daniel Everett, a linguist, lives among the Pirahã, a people of the Brazilian Amazon settled along the Maici River, whose language has between 250 and 380 speakers. According to his account, the Pirahã, worried about being cheated in their trade dealings, ask him to teach them arithmetic. After eight months of daily study, none has learned to count to ten, or even to add 1 + 1, and the classes stop.

## A Language Without Number Words

Everett first described two words, hói and hoí, distinguished by tone, as “one” and “two.” In his 2005 analysis, he instead places them among terms for “small quantity” and “larger quantity.” Frank and colleagues conclude in 2008 that they are much more likely relative terms, like “few” or “less,” than absolute terms like “one.” In 2004, the psycholinguist Peter Gordon, who describes a “one-two-many” system, tested what this language changes in the perception of quantities: he asked Pirahã speakers to reproduce rows of objects, notably batteries, laid out by the experimenter. Performance is good for small quantities, then becomes remarkably poor beyond three objects, with a constant coefficient of variation: the error grows with the quantity. Gordon reads this as the sign of approximate, analog estimation rather than exact counting: the kind of assessment anyone uses to tell “a few” objects from “many,” without counting them one by one.

## A Language Without Embedding?

In his 2005 article, Everett goes further: he argues that Pirahã also lacks grammatical recursion, the ability to embed one clause inside another, considered since Noam Chomsky to be a universal feature of human language. If this absence were real, it would make recursion a falsified universal. Chomsky maintains, however, that even if Pirahã had all the properties Everett described, it would have no implications for universal grammar. In 2009, the linguists Andrew Nevins, David Pesetsky, and Cilene Rodrigues published a reassessment: they claim that recursion had been observed in Pirahã by Everett himself, in his earlier work that interpreted the suffix -sai as an embedding. Everett replies that his understanding at the time was incomplete and biased by a theoretical preconception, and that -sai merely marks old information.

## What Remains Solid, What Remains Disputed

One point withstands the controversy: the studies cited agree that Pirahã does without exact number words. Beyond that foundation, the results themselves diverge from one study to the next. Frank, Everett, Fedorenko, and Gibson (2008), who reuse Gordon's tasks, report that Pirahã speakers succeed at exact matching, even with large quantities, but go wrong as soon as the task calls on memory. Frank, Fedorenko, Lai, Saxe, and Gibson (2012) show, for their part, that English speakers whose access to number words is blocked by a verbal interference task fall back on the same analog estimation. Caleb Everett and Keren Madora (2012) do not find the 2008 success: their participants cannot consistently match quantities above three, even with no recall or transposition requirement whatsoever. The authors suggest that earlier counting training, received by the participants in the 2008 study, might explain the gap. The question is therefore no longer only whether this language goes without numbers, but what that lack actually changes about what its speakers can think, and the studies themselves do not yet agree on the size of that effect.

repere.texte: In Peter Gordon's matching tasks, Pirahã speakers show remarkably poor performance with quantities above three, but with a coefficient of variation that remains constant: which suggests analog estimation.
repere.source: Peter Gordon, “Numerical Cognition Without Words: Evidence from Amazonia,” Science, vol. 306, no. 5695, 2004, pp. 496-499

carte.punch: Eight months of classes requested by the Pirahã: none learned to count to ten.
carte.idee: Pirahã, a language of the Amazon, has no exact number word. A 2004 study reports remarkably poor performance beyond three objects, of the approximate-estimation type; later studies diverge on what this reveals.

quiz.question: What does the matching task run by Peter Gordon with Pirahã speakers show?
choix: That they perceive no difference between quantities, even the smallest
That they manage with small quantities, but that their performance becomes very poor beyond three objects
That they count as precisely as any speaker who has number words
That their language lets them distinguish only the singular from the plural
quiz.explication: Gordon reports good performance for small quantities, then remarkably poor performance beyond three objects, with a constant coefficient of variation: a sign, in his view, of analog estimation rather than exact counting. The other three propositions go beyond what the study shows: small quantities are perceived, precision does not reach that of counting, and nothing concerns the singular and the plural.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Daniel Everett observe when he tried, at their request, to teach arithmetic to the Pirahã?
choix: That after eight months of daily study, none had learned to count to ten
That half of the students learned to count to one hundred
That only the children succeeded in learning to count
That the Pirahã refused to attend the classes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Everett's account, the Pirahã, worried about being cheated in their trade dealings, had asked for these classes; after eight months, none had learned to count to ten or to add 1 + 1. Everett points in particular to the absence of any need for exact counting in their way of life. The other propositions are false: no one got as far as one hundred, the children did no better, and it was the Pirahã who had asked for the classes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the disagreement between Daniel Everett and the linguists Nevins, Pesetsky, and Rodrigues about?
choix: The very existence of the Pirahã people
Whether or not grammatical recursion is present in the Pirahã language
The exact number of speakers still living
The translation of the name of the Maici River
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Everett maintains that the absence of recursion (or embedding) in Pirahã contradicts the idea of a universal grammar; Nevins, Pesetsky, and Rodrigues (2009) claim, on the contrary, to have found traces of recursion in his own data.
